theme: Doctrinal Pause: The New Heavens and New Earth
doctrine: The New Heavens and New Earth
summary: The renewal of all things; the resurrection life in a transformed creation; God dwelling with his people
readingInstruction: Read Revelation 21:1-22:5, Isaiah 65:17-25, and 2 Peter 3:10-13. Today is a doctrinal pause on the new heavens and new earth: the final destiny of believers and of creation. Notice how the Old Testament prophecy, Peter’s teaching, and John’s vision fit together.
settingTheScene: What is heaven like? Many Christians imagine the final state as a spiritual realm where disembodied souls float on clouds, but the Bible’s picture is richer and more physical. The final hope of the believer is not escaping the world but a renewed world, with resurrected bodies in a restored creation, in which God dwells with his people. Getting this right shapes how we value creation, work, and our present life.
observation: “For behold, I create new heavens and a new earth, and the former things shall not be remembered or come into mind” (Isaiah 65:17).
“They shall build houses and inhabit them; they shall plant vineyards and eat their fruit” (Isaiah 65:21).
“The wolf and the lamb shall graze together” (Isaiah 65:25).
“The day of the Lord will come like a thief” (2 Peter 3:10).
“But according to his promise we are waiting for new heavens and a new earth in which righteousness dwells” (2 Peter 3:13).
“Then I saw a new heaven and a new earth” (Revelation 21:1).
“Behold, I am making all things new” (Revelation 21:5).
“The throne of God and of the Lamb will be in it, and his servants will worship him” (Revelation 22:3).
doctrinalFocus:
The Bible’s final hope is the new heavens and new earth. Four features stand out.

First, it is a renewed creation, not a mere escape. God created the world and called it very good. The fall corrupted it, but God does not abandon his creation. Paul says that “the creation itself will be set free from its bondage to corruption and obtain the freedom of the glory of the children of God” (Romans 8:21). Christ’s death and resurrection are the first fruits of the renewal of all things (Colossians 1:20). Christians differ on how much continuity there is between the present creation and the new one. Many Reformed teachers hold that the new earth will be a purification and renewal of this one (as the flood cleansed but did not destroy the earth), while some, including many Lutherans, hold that God will annihilate the present world and create a wholly new one. In either case, the new creation is physical, real, and glorious, and what we do now in faith is not in vain (1 Corinthians 15:58).

Second, it includes the resurrection of the body. We will not be disembodied spirits. When Christ returns, the dead in Christ will be raised, and the living changed, so that we have glorified bodies like his (Philippians 3:20-21; 1 Corinthians 15:42-54). Those who die before then are “with Christ, which is far better” (Philippians 1:23) in a conscious intermediate state, as we saw in Unit 21, but the final hope is resurrection on the new earth.

Third, it is the fulfillment of the covenants. In Genesis 1-2, God made humanity to dwell with him in a garden and to rule creation. Abraham was promised land, and Paul says he was promised “the world” (Romans 4:13). The Israelites who longed for the promised land were looking toward “a better country, that is, a heavenly one” (Hebrews 11:16), “the city that has foundations” (Hebrews 11:10). David’s throne is fulfilled in the reign of Christ. The new covenant, with its promise of forgiveness and God dwelling with his people, comes to its full fruition. In progressive covenantalism, all the covenants find their fulfillment in Christ and his people in the new creation: the land becomes the whole earth, the temple becomes God’s presence with all, and the people of God are drawn from all nations.

Fourth, it is a place of worship, rest, work, and joy. The picture includes seeing God’s face (Revelation 22:4), the absence of sin, death, and tears, the reign of the saints with Christ (22:5), the healing of the nations, and the glory of the nations being brought in (21:24-26). Isaiah 65 includes houses, vineyards, and long life, which suggests meaningful work and enjoyment, without frustration. There will be rest, as the Sabbath points forward (Hebrews 4:9-11). The center of it all is God himself. As the old catechism says, our chief end is to glorify God and enjoy him forever.

So how should this hope shape us? It gives us courage in suffering (Romans 8:18), motivates holy living (2 Peter 3:11-14), directs our affections toward the things above (Colossians 3:1-4), and prompts us to care for the creation that God will renew. It gives dignity to the work we do now. And it fills us with longing: “Come, Lord Jesus!”
interpretation:
Isaiah 65 is the Old Testament source. God promises new heavens and a new earth, and Jerusalem as a joy. The former things will be forgotten. There will be no more weeping, no more infant mortality, and people will live long. They will build houses and inhabit them, plant vineyards and eat their fruit, no longer for others to take. The wolf and the lamb will graze together; the lion shall eat straw like the ox, and “they shall not hurt or destroy in all my holy mountain.” This is a picture of peace, justice, and flourishing. John in Revelation 21 sees the fulfillment on a larger scale.

Peter, in 2 Peter 3, addresses scoffers who say that all things continue as they were. He declares that the day of the Lord will come like a thief, with the heavens passing away with a roar, and the elements dissolved with heat. As we saw on Day 852, this can be read as the purging of the creation by fire. And then the application: “Since all these things are thus to be dissolved, what sort of people ought you to be in lives of holiness and godliness, waiting for and hastening the coming of the day of God?” The hope is the incentive to holiness.

Taken together, these passages show that Christians are not waiting for evacuation but for new creation. Paul’s, Peter’s, Isaiah’s, and John’s visions harmonize: the world will be made right, and God will dwell here with his people.
connection: Genesis 1:31, 3:17-19, and Romans 8:18-25 trace creation, fall, and redemption. Colossians 1:15-20 and Ephesians 1:9-10 speak of reconciling all things in Christ. Matthew 19:28 mentions the renewal of all things. Acts 3:21 speaks of the restoration of all things. Philippians 3:20-21 and 1 Corinthians 15:35-58 speak of resurrection bodies. Psalm 37:11 and Matthew 5:5 promise the meek will inherit the earth. Hebrews 11:8-16 and Romans 4:13 speak of the promised world. 1 Thessalonians 4:13-18 describes Christ’s return. Habakkuk 2:14 and Isaiah 11:6-9 describe the earth filled with the knowledge of the LORD.
application:
Think about what you imagined heaven would be like. How does the picture of a renewed earth change it?

Choose one way to care for God’s creation this week (a neighbor’s yard, a garden, a recycling habit, a walk), as an expression of hope.

Do some of your normal work today as something that will not be wasted in God’s new world.
prayerPrompts: Thank God for the promise of new heavens and a new earth.
Ask him to help you live as a citizen of that world now.
Tell him what you long for there.
